stages.name: Mecca — Refusal & Departure
stages.shortDesc: Imam Hussain (AS) refuses to pledge allegiance to Yazid and departs the Holy City.
stages.desc:
Yazid ibn Muawiyah demanded a public oath of allegiance from Imam Hussain (AS) — grandson of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH&HF). To pledge allegiance to a man known for tyranny and openly sinful conduct would have been to legitimise evil with the weight of prophetic lineage. The Imam refused absolutely.

Fearing assassination within the sacred precincts of Mecca — which would have desecrated the Haram itself — Imam Hussain (AS) departed on the Day of Tarwiyah, the 8th of Dhul-Hijjah, cutting short his Hajj pilgrimage. His departure was a profound sacrifice: leaving the holiest city on Earth to preserve its sanctity, and to answer the thousands of letters that had poured in from the people of Kufa, who pledged loyalty and begged him to come lead them against injustice.

He had already sent his cousin Muslim ibn Aqeel ahead to Kufa to verify the sincerity of the pledges. Muslim's reports confirmed extraordinary support — over eighteen thousand had sworn allegiance.
figures: Muslim ibn Aqeel (sent ahead to Kufa)
stages.quote: I have not risen up for corruption, nor for amusement, nor for pride or oppression. I have only risen to seek reform in the nation of my grandfather. I wish to command good and forbid evil.
stages.quoteAttr: Imam Hussain (AS), in his will before departing Mecca

stages.name: Medina — Farewell to the Prophet
stages.shortDesc: The Imam bids farewell at his grandfather's tomb and gathers his family.
stages.desc:
Before the journey northward, Imam Hussain (AS) had spent time in Medina, the city of his grandfather the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH&HF). Here he had visited the Prophet's blessed tomb — a farewell that carried the weight of all that was to come. He wept at the tomb and communed with the Prophet in prayer through the night.

It was in Medina that the letters from Kufa had begun arriving, carried by secret messengers — first dozens, then hundreds, then thousands. 'Come to us,' they said. 'We have no Imam. God will guide the truth through you.' The Imam responded by sending Muslim ibn Aqeel to verify the situation.

Now, with his family gathered — women, children, the aged — the Imam made his final farewell to Medina. The city he loved, the city of the Prophet, the city that held his mother Fatima al-Zahra (AS) in its earth. He would not see it again.
stages.quote: O God, this is the tomb of Your Prophet, and I am the son of Your Prophet's daughter. You know what I am facing. O God, I love what is good and hate what is evil.
stages.quoteAttr: Attributed to Imam Hussain (AS), at the Prophet's tomb in Medina

stages.name: Thaʿlabiyya — The Truth Arrives
stages.shortDesc: News arrives: Muslim ibn Aqeel has been martyred. The Imam speaks truth to his companions.
stages.desc:
Deep in the desert at the watering station of Thaʿlabiyya, a rider arrived with devastating news. Muslim ibn Aqeel — the Imam's cousin, emissary, and trusted companion — had been captured in Kufa. The governor Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad had crushed the uprising. Muslim was tortured and thrown from the palace rooftop. Hani ibn Urwa, who had sheltered him, was also killed.

The movement in Kufa was destroyed. The very city that had sent eighteen thousand pledges of loyalty had abandoned Muslim when the moment of truth arrived.

Imam Hussain (AS) gathered every companion and spoke plainly. He told them what had happened without softening the truth. He declared that whoever had come hoping for political victory was free to leave — all pledges were released, all obligations lifted. He held no grievance.

The desert night filled with the sound of departures. Horses moving away in the dark. Those who remained by morning had chosen something entirely different from what they had imagined when they set out. They were not going to a victory. They were going to a testimony.
stages.quote: I do not see death except as prosperity, and life among the unjust except as grief and suffering.
stages.quoteAttr: Imam Hussain (AS), upon receiving news at Thaʿlabiyya

stages.name: Zubalah — The Messenger Falls
stages.shortDesc: Another martyr: Qays ibn Mushir is executed for refusing to denounce the Imam.
stages.desc:
At Zubalah, an ancient caravan town on the pilgrimage road to Kufa, another messenger arrived. Qays ibn Mushir al-Saydawi — dispatched by the Imam with a letter to the people of Kufa — had been captured by Ibn Ziyad's forces. When brought before the governor and ordered to denounce Imam Hussain (AS) from the pulpit, Qays instead praised the Imam openly and called curses upon Yazid. He was thrown from the rooftop.

Abdullah ibn Yaqtur, another messenger, had also been killed.

When the Imam heard this, his eyes filled with tears. He then recited from the Quran: 'Among the believers are men who have been true to the covenant they made with God. Some have fulfilled that vow through death, and some are still waiting.' He raised no army of revenge. He did not turn back. He continued northward, toward a place whose name he already knew.
stages.quote: Among the believers are men who have been true to the covenant they made with God. Some of them have fulfilled their vow by death, and some are still waiting — they have not changed in the least.
stages.quoteAttr: Quran 33:23, recited by Imam Hussain (AS) at Zubalah upon receiving news of Qays

stages.name: Sharaf — One Thousand Horsemen
stages.shortDesc: Hurr ibn Yazid al-Riyahi arrives with 1,000 cavalry. The Imam gives them water.
stages.desc:
Before dawn at the water station of Sharaf, a companion climbed a hill and saw the horizon darken — not palm trees, but cavalry. One thousand horsemen under Hurr ibn Yazid al-Riyahi, the vanguard of Ibn Ziyad's forces, had intercepted the caravan.

Hurr's men were exhausted and thirsty from their desert crossing. In one of the most extraordinary moments of the journey, Imam Hussain (AS) gave the order: give water to every man and every horse — the very soldiers sent to stop him. Every person drank their fill. The horses were watered until satisfied.

At midday, Imam Hussain (AS) led the prayer. Hurr's entire army prayed behind him — the leader they were ordered to capture, leading the prayer of those sent to capture him.

Hurr had orders to deliver the Imam to Kufa or prevent his return to Mecca. But he had received no order to attack. An uneasy parallel march began, the two groups moving side by side across the plain — one free, one their captor, both uncertain of what came next.
stages.quote: O people! If you are fearful of God and recognise the rights of those who deserve them, God will be more pleased with you. We, the household of Muhammad, are more deserving of authority over you than those who claim it without right.
stages.quoteAttr: Imam Hussain (AS), speaking to Hurr's army at Sharaf

stages.name: ʿUdhayb al-Hijanat — Last Free Companions
stages.shortDesc: Four men slip from Kufa to join the Imam — the last companions to arrive freely.
stages.desc:
At the way-station of ʿUdhayb al-Hijanat, four men rode in from the direction of Kufa — Nafi ibn Hilal al-Jamali, Hajjaj ibn Masruq al-Juʿfi, and their companions. They had slipped past the governor's patrols at night, riding hard across the desert to reach the Imam.

They brought the clearest picture yet of Kufa: Ibn Ziyad controlled the city absolutely. Supporters of the Imam were under surveillance, imprisoned, or executed. There would be no army waiting, no city gates opening in welcome.

These four men knew all of this. They came anyway.

It was here also that the poet Farazdaq gave the Imam his famous assessment: 'Their hearts are with you, but their swords will be drawn against you.' The Imam received the words without bitterness. He understood. He had understood for some time.

These were the last companions to join the caravan as free men making a free choice. Those who came after would have no road back.
stages.quote: Their hearts are with you, but their swords will be drawn against you tomorrow.
stages.quoteAttr: The poet Farazdaq to Imam Hussain (AS), at ʿUdhayb al-Hijanat

stages.name: Ninawa — Forced to a Halt
stages.shortDesc: Ibn Ziyad orders the caravan stopped in open desert. The Karbala plain is reached.
stages.desc:
A rider arrived at speed carrying a letter from governor Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad directly to Hurr ibn Yazid. The order was precise and deliberate: halt the caravan of Hussain (AS) — not near any city, not near water, but in open, exposed desert.

Ibn Ziyad had dispatched a much larger army under the command of Umar ibn Saʿd, son of the famed companion Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas. Umar was a reluctant general — he had initially refused the commission — but Ibn Ziyad had threatened to strip him of his governorship. He came with thirty thousand men.

Hurr communicated the order to the Imam with visible discomfort. Zuhayr ibn Qayn urged Imam Hussain (AS) to fight Hurr's smaller force now, before the larger army arrived. The Imam refused: 'I will not be the first to raise a sword.' He would not strike the first blow.

The caravan moved a short distance further east, to the flat, treeless plain beside the Euphrates. On the 2nd of Muharram, 61 AH, they stopped. The place was called Karbala.
stages.quote: I can see nothing ahead of us but death. But by God, I do not care whether we go to death or death comes to us.
stages.quoteAttr: Imam Hussain (AS), at the approach to the plain of Karbala

stages.name: Karbala — The Eternal Stand
stages.shortDesc: 72 souls stand against 30,000. The day that divided history. Truth against power.
stages.desc:
On the 2nd of Muharram the caravan reached Karbala — a word whose Arabic roots carry the meanings of sorrow (karb) and trial (bala). The Euphrates flowed within sight. On the 7th of Muharram, by order of Ibn Ziyad, Umar ibn Saʿd's army cut off access to the water. The camp's children cried from thirst. The infant Ali al-Asghar could not feed.

On the eve of Ashura, Imam Hussain (AS) extinguished all the torches in the camp. In darkness, so no one could see another's tears, he addressed his companions a final time. He released them completely — every pledge, every obligation. He told them to take his family and go. 'They want me,' he said. 'Not you.'

One by one, voices rose in the dark. His son Ali al-Akbar: 'Are we to live after you?' His brother Abbas: 'How could we abandon you?' Zuhayr ibn Qayn: 'I wish I could die a thousand times and return a thousand times for you.' Habib ibn Muzahir wept silently. Hurr ibn Yazid — who had blocked the Imam's road — rode over from the enemy camp that morning, trembling: 'I am the one who stopped your path. I seek your forgiveness.' The Imam embraced him.

On the morning of Ashura, the 10th of Muharram, the battle began. The 72 companions fell one by one across the morning hours. The Imam buried each one himself with his own hands, praying over every body. By the time of afternoon prayer, he stood alone on the plain. He called out: 'Is there anyone to help us? Is there anyone to defend the household of the Prophet?' The earth gave no answer.

He was martyred as the sun moved toward the west. His head was raised on a spear. The camp was burned. The women and children — Lady Zaynab, Lady Umm Kulthum, the sick Ali ibn Hussain — were taken captive to Kufa, then to Damascus.

But Lady Zaynab (AS) stood in the court of Yazid himself and declared: 'Do your worst. By God, you shall never erase our memory.' She was right. Fourteen centuries have not erased it.
figures: Hurr ibn Yazid al-Riyahi — redeemed, first martyr
Abbas ibn Ali — martyred at the Euphrates
Lady Zaynab (AS) — survived, carried the message
Imam Ali ibn Hussain / Zayn al-Abidin (AS) — ill, survived, continued the Imamate
stages.quote: On the Day of Judgement, no eye will weep save the eye that wept for Hussain — and every eye will grieve on that day, except the eye that shed tears for Hussain.
